g.2: Step-by-step decoder of the Voyager Golden Record — from the cover to the first image.
s0.2: The Golden Record left in 1977 aboard the Voyager 1 and 2 probes: a gold-plated copper phonograph record, 30 cm (12″) across. It has no “player” built in. All a finder has is the cover, engraved with instruction diagrams and no words.
s0.3: 115 images, stored as an analog audio signal
s0.4: greetings in 55 languages, “Sounds of the Earth”, about 90 minutes of music
s0.5: played from the edge toward the center, at 16⅔ revolutions/minute
s0.6: Tap an area of the diagram below (our own simplified diagram, not a reproduction of the cover).
s1.2: The cover shows the record and the stylus, and the rotation diagram marks one full turn in a given time. The correct speed is 16⅔ rpm. Try other speeds and see what happens to the signal.
s1.5: Why it matters. The whole decoder rests on a single number: one image line lasts 8 ms. If playback runs twice as fast, the line lasts 4 ms, and the image falls apart if you keep assuming 8 ms. The circle in step 6 lets you check this.
s2.2: How do you communicate a duration without a common language? The cover uses a physical phenomenon known to any technical civilization: the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen (the electron spin flip), at 1420.405751768 MHz, that is, a wavelength of ≈21 cm. Its period is the cover's unit of time. All durations are written as binary multiples of this period.
s3.2: The cover carries a map of 14 pulsars, drawn as lines radiating from the same point (the Sun). The length of a line is the relative distance. On each one, the pulsar's period is written as a binary number of hydrogen units. Pulsars slow down gradually and predictably, so the period measured today, compared with the one on the cover, gives the launch date.
s3.3: Below you can do the conversion shown on the cover. The examples are real periods, rounded.
s4.2: An image is divided into 512 vertical lines. Each line is an 8 ms slice of signal, and the amplitude encodes brightness (white = high amplitude). At 48 kHz, 8 ms means 384 samples, that is, 384 “pixels” per line. The whole image lasts 512 × 8 ms ≈ 4.1 s.
s4.3: The images in the app are schematic, generated here for demonstration (they are not the NASA ones). Loading the real recording is done in step 9.
s5.2: The first image on the record is a circle. Its purpose: if the circle comes out round after decoding, you have the right line duration and proportions. Here you have the circle's signal and a parameter that is wrong from the start: the assumed sampling rate (44100 Hz instead of 48000 Hz). Correct it with the slider or let the app search for it.
s5.3: Assumed rate: Hz → samples/line
s5.7: Automatic calibration does two things: it estimates L from the signal's autocorrelation (precision of about one sample), then refines it by the roundness of the circle (precision of ~0.002). Without a circle in the signal, only the first stage is available.
s6.2: See how the image is built: at the top, the waveform of the current line (384 samples); at the bottom, the image reconstructed up to that line.
s7.2: Color images are three consecutive images, each one brightness through a filter (red, green, blue). You decode them separately and combine them.
s7.10: If the order is wrong, the sky turns orange and the leaves red: same signal, misread.
s8.2: Load an audio file (WAV, FLAC, MP3, OGG) that contains a segment with the record's images. The whole process stays local, in the browser, with nothing sent over the network. For very long files, use a segment of a few minutes (browser memory is limited).
s8.3: Tap the waveform to move the start of the image.
s9c.2: The 2026–2027 record can also carry people's voices. Anyone can submit a written greeting, an image or a voice message (up to 15 s), any one of them or all three. There is no server: everything you do stays on your device until you send the package file to the organizer yourself.
s9c.3: Send only what is yours or what you have the right to pass on.
s9c.4: No advertising, hate or other people's personal data. Images of people only with their consent.
s9c.5: The message may be read thousands of years from now: short, clear, peaceful.
s9c.6: The organizer may reject any contribution.
s9c.10: My name may appear in the contributors' register (otherwise I stay anonymous)
s9c.31: The contribution is mine or I have the right to pass it on, and the recognizable people in it agree.
s9c.32: I agree to it being included on the probe's record and published under the chosen license.
s9c.36: The package is a .json file. Send it to the organizer (the address is in the e-mail button); the app does not send it anywhere by itself.
s9c.37: For the organizer: if you host this file, share its address followed by #contribute. It opens directly on this page, without the rest of the steps.
s9e.2: Now you cross to the other side: you build the record of a probe launched in 2026–2027. The encoding function does exactly the opposite of the decoder: it scales each image to 512×384, turns brightness into amplitude (one column = 8 ms = 384 samples at 48 kHz) and lines them up in order. The first is the calibration circle; color goes in three frames, R, G, B.
s9e.3: Everything stays in the browser. The result: a 48 kHz, 16-bit, mono WAV, plus an index with the start times. Each image is decoded back from the quantized signal, so you can see whether it survives.
s9e.13: The text page is rendered as an image, so any decoder that reads images can read it too.
s9e.15: Import the packages (.json) sent by the public from the “Contribute” step. Only packages with explicit consent are accepted. Check each contribution before ticking it.
s9e.18: Add the ticked ones to the record
s9e.21: Music is not included in the app. You upload an audio file you have the right to use, fill in the rights sheet, and the app puts it on the record (stereo WAV, 48 kHz) and lists it in the index. A track with unclear rights cannot be added.
s9e.23: Another track or your own performance
s9e.33: License obtained for composition and recording
s9e.34: Own performance + license obtained for the composition
s9e.35: Own performance of a public-domain composition
s9e.38: e.g. contract no., e-mail, page address
s9e.43: The periods are extrapolated linearly from approximate reference values (epoch 2020). For a real record, use the periods measured from the ATNF catalogue for all 14 pulsars.
s9.2: The inventory of the Voyager Interstellar Record (the Golden Record), attached to the Voyager 1 and 2 probes. The sources are Wikipedia (“Contents of the Voyager Golden Record”, “Voyager Golden Record”) and the Ozma Records page. The rights classification in the table is my own, indicative, not an official NASA table.
s9.4: A old composition (public domain in most countries), the modern recording remains protected · B traditional / field or archive recording · C commercial composition and recording, license required · D 1927 recording, in the US probably public domain (95-year rule, to be verified).
s9.6: The English greeting by UN Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim opens the spoken part. Greetings in 55 languages follow (recorded at Cornell), in the order on the record, and the last one, in English, is by Nick Sagan.
s9.8: Sound montage made by Ann Druyan and team (list from memory, to be verified in NASA sources):
s9.9: nature: volcanoes, earthquake, thunder, mud pots, wind, rain, surf, crickets, frogs, birds, hyena, elephant, chimpanzee, wild dog
s9.10: humans and technology: footsteps and heartbeats, laughter, fire, first tools, tame dog, blacksmith, saw, tractor, ships, horse and cart, train, truck, car, bus, motorcycle, airplane, Saturn V
s9.11: Morse code with per aspera ad astra; a kiss; mother and child
s9.12: “Signs of Life”: ~1 hour of Ann Druyan's heartbeats and brainwaves, compressed to ~1 minute
s9.13: humpback whale song, from Roger Payne's recordings (the album Songs of the Humpback Whale, 1970)
s9.15: Wikipedia counts 116 images, one of which is the calibration circle (so 115 of content); Carter's statement appears in addition, encoded as images.
s9.16: calibration and references: the circle, the map of the Sun's location, mathematical and unit definitions, Solar System parameters
s9.17: Sun, solar spectrum, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, Earth; Egypt–Red Sea–Nile
s9.18: chemistry, DNA, cells and division; human anatomy (8 diagrams)
s9.20: continental drift, Earth's structure, vertebrate evolution
s9.21: landscapes, plants and animals (reef, beaches, rivers, deserts, forests, dolphins, crocodile, eagle)
s9.22: Jane Goodall with chimpanzees and people from around the world; activities (mountaineering, gymnastics, school, harvest, supermarket, cooking, meal)
s9.23: architecture and cities (Great Wall, Taj Mahal, Oxford, Boston, UN, Sydney Opera House)
s9.24: industry and transport (factory, museum, X-ray, microscope, highways, Golden Gate, train, airplane, airport)
s9.25: exploration and science (Antarctic expedition, radio telescopes, page from Newton, astronaut Ed White, Titan Centaur launch)
s9.26: sunset with birds, string quartet, violin with sheet music
s9.28: Kurt Waldheim, UN Secretary-General: spoken greeting in English
s9.29: Jimmy Carter, President of the USA: written statement, encoded as images
s9.30: Copyright · what we know and what we don't
s9.31: A record like this combines four kinds of rights: the composition (author, publisher), the recording (performers, record label), the images (photographer, agency) and the field recordings (archive, community). In the EU and in Romania, protection of a composition lasts for the author's life + 70 years.
s9.32: We did not find a public, official table of the licensing agreements for each track and image. The sources consulted do not say who holds the rights to each element, nor what terms NASA had.
s9.33: For the images, the sources say they were included “when copyright allowed”; many are credited to photographers and agencies (for example Ansel Adams, Stephen Dalton, sources linked to National Geographic). The photograph of a nude couple was replaced with a silhouette.
s9.34: NASA uploaded the audio to SoundCloud in 2015. Being publicly listenable does not mean a reuse license.
s9.35: The 2017 Ozma Records reissue (a Kickstarter of over $1.4 million, a 2018 Grammy for packaging) did exist, but its license terms are not described in the sources consulted.
s9.36: “Here Comes the Sun” (Beatles, 1969, George Harrison): Sagan wanted the song. In Murmurs of Earth (1978) he writes that the Beatles were in favor, but “did not own the rights, and the legal status seemed too unclear to risk”. EMI, which held the rights, refused. Ann Druyan recounted in 2015 that EMI had asked for $50,000 per recording, for two, while the whole record had cost $18,000. Timothy Ferris disputed in 2017 that the song was ever seriously considered.
s9.37: This is not legal advice. For any reuse, check each element with the rights holder.

title: BRAZDA — the Voyager Golden Record decoder
hd.desc: BRAZDA: step-by-step decoder and encoder for the Voyager Golden Record, in a single HTML file, offline.
hd.ogt: BRAZDA — the Voyager Golden Record decoder
hd.ogd: From the cover to the first image, and back: encode the record of a 2026–2027 probe.
i0.1: The record. Gold-plated copper, 30 cm. The groove (the spiral) starts at the edge and runs toward the center. For preservation in vacuum, the record is enclosed in an aluminum cover. On the cover, a cartridge and a stylus are mounted next to it.
i0.2: The stylus. The diagram shows how the stylus sits on the groove and how the record turns. Without the stylus in the correct position nothing is heard. The speed (16⅔ rpm) is given by a cycle drawn on the cover.
i0.3: Hydrogen. Two hydrogen atoms with opposite spins: the transition between the two states emits the 21 cm wave. Its period ≈ 0.704 ns is the unit of time for the whole cover (step 3).
i0.4: The circle image. The first image on the record is a circle. The diagram shows how each vertical line of the image corresponds to an 8 ms slice of signal. The number of lines (512) is written in binary. See steps 5–7.
i0.5: The pulsars. The map of 14 pulsars shows where the Sun is relative to them, and their periods also indicate the moment of launch (step 4).

m.hcts:
Here Comes the Sun · composition by George Harrison, 1969 (Abbey Road). The song is still protected: the author died in 2001, and in the EU protection lasts until the end of 2071.
For the original Beatles recording you need a license for the composition AND for the recording, from two different holders. For your own performance you only need the composition license.
In 1977, the Sagan team asked for the song for the Golden Record, and EMI refused (Druyan: $50,000 per recording, for two; Ferris disputes that it was seriously considered). The app does not contain the song and cannot add it without a license.

s12.2: Voyager 1 is closing in on one light-day from Earth: 25,902,068,371 km, the distance light travels in a day. The figures below are computed in the page, offline, from a model calibrated on published values (see “How it is computed”).
s12.10: One full turn = one light-day (24 light-hours). The gold arc is Voyager 1, the blue one is Voyager 2 (estimate).
s12.12: A message sent from Earth now reaches each target after its flight time. Move the slider or press “Play the ray”. The time scale is logarithmic, from 1 s to 26 h.
s12.16: The model. The probe moves almost in a straight line relative to the Sun (Voyager 1: ~16.95 km/s, towards ecliptic +35°), and Earth’s position comes from low-precision astronomical formulas. The Voyager 1 values are calibrated on published milestones:
s12.17: the one-light-day threshold (25,902,068,371 km) on 18 November 2026, 10:16:07 UTC;
s12.18: the distance grows until ~21 January 2027, shrinks until ~24 April 2027 and stops at ~1.0010 light-days, so the threshold is crossed only once;
s12.19: one light-day from the Sun around ~3 February 2027;
s12.20: the speed relative to Earth oscillates between ~−7.6 and ~+41 km/s.
s12.21: Accuracy. The app checks its model against these milestones (the exact threshold moment, the extremes within a few days). The deviation from the official JPL Horizons ephemerides was not measured here: treat the last digits of the distance as illustrative, not as a measurement. Voyager 2 is a coarser estimate (±1 AU), with approximate direction and starting point.
s12.22: Sources: NASA, “What is a light-day?” · EarthSky, EarthSky, 18 November 2026 · parsec.ro, “A light-day from Earth” (calibration milestones) · JPL Horizons.
s12.25: Voyager carries a disc that nobody in its world can read. The next step is to see how it would be read.
s12.26: Voyager 1 crosses the one-light-day threshold only once, then the distance keeps oscillating with Earth’s motion.
